title: I'm building a Bannerlord + Crusader Kings-style sandbox in the browser, solo, with Claude Code and Codex. Here's the workflow that's actually kept it from collapsing
author: Ivaricus
selftext:
Hello everyone. I'm making Houses of Veyra, a feudal sci-fi sandbox in Godot 4. You lead a minor noble house around an overworld map, recruit a warband, fight real-time squad battles, and deal with politics: marriages, heirs, rival houses, wars. It runs in the browser on [itch.io](http://itch.io), and on mobile too.

I'm a solo dev, and most of the code has been written with AI coding agents (Codex first, now mostly Claude Code). The project is pretty big now: the main campaign state file alone is around 14k lines. I wanted to share what's worked, because "just ask the AI to make a game" falls apart fast at this size.

What's kept it sane:

\- A design doc and a roadmap first. The AI works from milestones (M0 to M14), not vibes. Each one is small and concrete.

\- Checkpoint files. After every stage the agent updates a markdown log: what changed, why, and what's still open. A new session reads the newest checkpoint and picks up where the last one stopped. This was the biggest win for me.

\- A test for every behaviour change. The project has about 166 headless Godot tests. The agent runs the focused test, then the nearby ones, then a smoke test. AI code that looks right but quietly breaks a save file is the real danger, and tests catch it.

\- Save compatibility rules. Any new persistent field needs init, save, load, a default for old saves, and a round-trip test. I learned that one the hard way.

\- Plan, approve, build. For new features the agent writes a short plan first and I approve it before any code gets written. It saves a lot of "wait, why did you rewrite the combat system" moments.

\- A project guide file (CLAUDE.md) that tells the agent where things live, which huge files to search instead of reading whole, and which tests are flaky.

Where AI still needs me:

\- Taste. It'll happily build a screen that's technically correct and has 40 lines of dense text on it. My latest update (a full readability pass) came from a Reddit player telling me exactly that.

\- Game feel and balance. It can't play the game, so I still do the playtesting.

\- Knowing when to stop adding systems.

The latest update has a full UI readability pass: coloured stance rings on the map so you can tell friend from foe, status chips in the header, a party roster, plain-language event odds, and a new pixel-art UI skin.

🎮 Play it in your browser: [https://jonnysoft.itch.io/houses-of-veyra](https://jonnysoft.itch.io/houses-of-veyra)

Happy to answer questions about the workflow, the testing setup, or how I keep the agent from wrecking a 14k-line file. And if you try the game, any feedback is welcome. I read all of it.
